section_title: How does a report from Paul’s nephew expose the ambush?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 12 When daylight came, the Jews formed a conspiracy and bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul. 13 More than forty of them were involved in this plot. 14 They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have bound ourselves with a solemn oath not to eat anything until we have killed Paul. 15 Now then, you and the Sanhedrin petition the commander to bring him down to you on the pretext of examining his case more carefully. We are ready to kill him on the way.”

16 But when the son of Paul’s sister heard about the plot, he went into the barracks and told Paul. 17 Then Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the commander; he has something to tell him.” 18 So the centurion took him to the commander and said, “Paul the prisoner sent and asked me to bring this young man to you. He has something to tell you.” 19 The commander took the young man by the hand, drew him aside, and asked, “What do you need to tell me?” 20 He answered, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul to the Sanhedrin tomorrow on the pretext of acquiring more information about him. 21 Do not let them persuade you, because more than forty men are waiting to ambush him. They have bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they have killed him; they are ready now, awaiting your consent.” 22 So the commander dismissed the young man and instructed him, “Do not tell anyone that you have reported this to me.”

context_lines: More than forty men bind themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul. They approach the chief priests and elders with a plan: the council should request another hearing as a pretext for a more thorough inquiry, while they wait to kill him on the way.

The oath uses **ἀναθεματίζω** (*anathematizō*, ah-nah-theh-mah-TEE-zoh), to bind oneself under a curse. [Thayer’s entry](https://biblehub.com/greek/332.htm) identifies that sense in Acts 23:12, 14 and 21. The men are invoking severe consequences on themselves, not merely making a casual promise. Luke does not tell us what becomes of the oath after the plot fails.

Paul’s sister’s son hears of the plot and tells him. Paul calls a centurion and has the young man taken to the commander, who draws him aside and listens privately. The nephew explains the false request and waiting ambush. The commander dismisses him with instructions not to disclose that he has reported it.

The young man’s report matters, but Luke does not tell us his exact age, where he heard the plan or whether his mother had been Paul’s host. His actions and the officials’ responses are enough to explain how the immediate threat becomes known.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read this as the exposure of a deliberate murder plot, not a legitimate conclusion to the hearing. The conspirators’ religiously serious oath does not make the intended killing just. The account also gives practical action a place: Paul passes on information rather than treating the Lord’s promise as a reason to do nothing.
god_plan_lines: The promise of witness in Rome comes immediately before this new attempt to kill Paul. Its protection now unfolds through a relative hearing the danger, Paul taking the report seriously and a commander listening. The narrative shows ordinary people and responsible action serving the continuation of the mission.

People who do not carry the public preaching role can still play an essential part in the work. The young man who brings information and the officer who listens help preserve the messenger for the task the Lord has given him.
